description_ru: Личное мнение о том, почему в эпоху электронных читалок и аудиокниг печатная книга остаётся незаменимой.
text:
Every few years, someone announces that the paper book is about to die. When the first e-readers appeared, journalists predicted that libraries would turn into museums and that children would never again know the smell of a new volume. More than a decade later, the e-reader has become a common sight on trains and beaches, but the paper book has refused to lie down. In many countries, printed books still account for the majority of sales. I do not think this is just nostalgia. I believe that there are good reasons why we should hold on to them.

Let me begin by admitting that e-readers are wonderful in many ways. Thousands of titles fit into a device that is lighter than a paperback. The type can be enlarged for people with poor eyesight, and a dictionary is only a tap away. I took one on a long journey last winter and was delighted not to have to choose between novels. If I were a student carrying six heavy textbooks, or a traveller with a strict weight limit, I would probably never go back. So this is not an argument against technology, but a defence of an old one.

The first reason is memory. A number of studies have suggested that people remember what they read on paper slightly better than what they read on a screen, particularly for long, complicated texts. One explanation is that a printed book has a physical shape. We know that an exciting scene was on the left-hand page, about a third of the way through, with a coffee stain in the corner. This sense of location helps the mind to organise what it has read. On a screen, the text just flows past, and every page looks exactly like every other.

The second reason is concentration. A tablet or a phone is a machine that was built to interrupt us. Even if you are reading a novel on it, the temptation of a message, a news alert or a quick look at the weather is only a swipe away. A paper book cannot send notifications. It asks for one thing only, which is your attention, and in return it offers a quiet corner of the world. A friend of mine, who works in advertising, told me that she had not finished a novel for years until she started leaving her phone in another room and picking up a paperback.

Then there is the question of ownership. When you buy a printed book, it is yours. You can lend it, give it away, sell it second-hand or leave it on a bench for a stranger to find. When you buy an electronic one, you often only buy a licence, and the company that sold it can, in theory, withdraw it or change the conditions. Some readers had an unpleasant surprise years ago when copies of a novel were deleted remotely from their devices. Ironically, the book in question was a story about a government that controlled what people were allowed to read.

A bookshelf is also a kind of autobiography. Visitors to my flat usually drift towards it, and a few minutes of browsing tell them more about me than an hour of conversation. The battered copies are the ones I have loved. The unread ones, which are many, are a gentle reproach. In my parents' house, my father's notes in the margins of his old textbooks are a way of hearing his voice. No digital file can offer that kind of intimacy, and a shelf of glowing icons does not carry the same weight.

It would be unfair to ignore the critics, who point out that paper is expensive, heavy and bad for the environment. Producing books does use trees, water and energy, and it is wasteful to print more copies than will be sold. Still, a book that is read by ten people, passed round a family and then donated to a charity shop has a much smaller footprint than a device that must be manufactured with rare metals and replaced every few years. The most environmentally friendly book is the one that already exists, and libraries make it possible for hundreds of people to share a single copy.

Libraries and bookshops, I should add, are the real heart of the matter. A bookshop is a place where you discover things you were not looking for. An algorithm may suggest more of what you have already enjoyed, but a shopkeeper will put a strange little novel into your hands and say that she thinks you will like it. This kind of accident is the source of many a lifelong passion. If paper books vanished, I suspect that the shops, and with them a certain kind of curiosity, would disappear too.

The future, I suspect, will not be a contest between paper and screen. Many readers already use both: an e-reader on a business trip, a paperback in the bath, an audiobook while cooking. That seems a healthy and sensible balance. But I hope that the printed book will always stay on the table, because it offers something that is increasingly rare: an object that does one thing, does it well and asks for nothing except that you turn the page.

focus_sounds.tip_ru: Тот же положение языка, что для θ, но с голосом: звук гудит, не «з».
Верхние зубы касаются нижней губы, голос включён; не «w» и не глухое «ф».
Ударение ставьте на нужный слог: ударный слог длиннее, громче и выше по тону, остальные сокращаются.
В конце слова и перед согласной «l» твёрдое: кончик языка вверху, спинка оттянута назад.

questions.question: What is the first reason the author gives for preferring paper?
questions.answer: People remember paper texts slightly better because a book has a physical shape and location.

questions.question: Why is a paper book better for concentration?
questions.answer: It cannot send notifications or messages.

questions.question: What is the problem with owning electronic books?
questions.answer: You only buy a licence and the company can withdraw the book.

questions.question: What does the author think the future will look like?
questions.answer: Readers will use both paper and screens.
